A corsage is a small, decorative arrangement of flowers — and sometimes ribbons, greenery, or other ornaments — that a person wears directly on their body as an accessory. Think of it as a tiny, wearable bouquet. It is not held in the hand like a regular bouquet; it is attached to the body.

A corsage is typically small enough to fit in the palm of your hand. It usually features one or a few flowers — such as roses, orchids, or carnations — often accompanied by small decorative elements like baby's breath (tiny white flowers), leaves, ribbon, or even small crystals or pearls. The overall look is neat, compact, and elegant.
Where on the Body Is It Worn?

A corsage is worn in one of two main ways:

  • Pinned to clothing — It is fastened with a pin onto a garment, most often near the chest, shoulder, or wrist area of a dress or jacket. This style is called a pin-on corsage.
  • On the wrist — It is worn like a bracelet, strapped or elasticated around the wrist. This is called a wrist corsage, and it is very popular today because it doesn't risk damaging the fabric of delicate clothing.
When and Why Is a Corsage Worn?

A corsage is worn on special, formal occasions. It is a symbol of celebration, honor, and affection. You would not typically wear one on an ordinary day. The most common occasions include:

  • Prom (a formal school dance) — This is perhaps the single most iconic use of the corsage in modern culture, especially in the United States. It is a longstanding tradition for a young man to gift his date a corsage on prom night. The corsage is coordinated to match her dress. In return, she typically gives him a boutonniere (a single small flower worn on his suit lapel — the small flap on the chest of a jacket).
  • Weddings — Mothers of the bride and groom, and sometimes bridesmaids, often wear corsages to mark their special role in the celebration.
  • Homecoming dances — Similar to prom, corsages are exchanged at these school formal events.
  • Other formal ceremonies — Graduations, anniversary parties, quinceañeras, and similar milestones where someone is being honored.

Corsages are traditionally worn by women, but this is a social tradition, not a rule. They are most commonly worn by:

  • A young woman attending a prom or formal dance.
  • The mother of the bride or groom at a wedding.
  • A woman being honored or celebrated at a special event.

Over time, as gender norms have evolved, corsages are sometimes worn by men at formal events as well, particularly at proms or weddings.

These two words are often seen together, so it helps to know the difference clearly:

  • A corsage is a small floral arrangement worn by a woman, typically on the wrist or chest.
  • A boutonniere is a single flower (or a very small cluster) worn by a man, pinned through the buttonhole or lapel of his suit jacket.

Both serve the same social purpose — they are floral accessories for formal occasions — but they differ in size, style, and the traditional gender of the wearer.

In older usage, and occasionally in fashion writing today, corsage can also refer to the bodice of a woman's dress — meaning the upper portion of the garment that covers the torso and chest. You might encounter this meaning in descriptions of historical or haute couture (high-end fashion) clothing. However, in everyday modern conversation, if someone says "corsage," they almost certainly mean the floral accessory, not part of a dress.
How to Think About It Simply

If you ever need a quick mental anchor: a corsage is a small, elegant flower arrangement that you wear on your body, given as a gift or gesture of honor on a formal occasion. It is most at home at a prom, a wedding, or any event where flowers, dressing up, and celebrating someone special all come together.
